# Debate: Four-day work week

- Mode: debate
- Cast: Amara Okafor (prop), Victor Hale (prop), Mei Tanaka-Ruiz (opp)
- Motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

**—**: ROUND 1 · OPENING

**Amara Okafor** [neutral]: Let's be honest about what a four-day week is not: it's not four longer days squeezed into the same rota. In our own wards, a compressed rota with guaranteed rest days cut burnout by about a fifth in twelve weeks, with patient throughput, length of stay and readmissions all within normal variation [^1]. What predicts staff exhaustion isn't total hours alone, it's the length of consecutive blocks, and four-day scheduling with protected rest breaks those blocks [^2]. High burnout in the ED climbed from 29% to 41% in ten months, and staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error [^2]. That's a patient safety argument, not a perk. A rested workforce is a safer one. I'll leave the macro numbers to Victor.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [neutral]: Opposition's case rests on three things. First, the pilots are promising on wellbeing, burnout down about a third and sick days down a fifth, but fewer than half the firms measured output consistently, so "revenue stayed flat" is a soft claim [^3]. Second, four-day weeks are not a uniform policy; they are a bundle of hours, pay, staffing and scheduling choices, and hospitals, transport and care cannot compress coverage the way a software firm can. The authors themselves recommend sector-specific trials before any national standard [^4]. Third, the second-order effect: someone absorbs the coordination, and in the pilots it was managers [^3] — that is cost, not magic. A national mandate would freeze one model before we know which sectors it breaks.

**Victor Hale** [neutral]: Three points, and I'll start with the one the opposition always concedes by accident: nobody here defends the five-day week as sacred. What Mei will defend is the calendar as we inherited it, and I invite the house to notice that the status quo is itself a policy choice that has to justify itself [^5] — so the burden is not mine alone. Second, the word "nationwide" means a default standard in law, not one identical rota for every ward, and "adopt" means legislate with a transition, exactly as the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default with a ten-year runway for agriculture and shipping [^6]. Third, the machinery already exists: continuous-coverage sectors run shift rules, rest periods, shift caps and averaging under Part IV of the Working Time Code, so a shorter standard week sits inside the structure rather than beside it. Keep your eye on what Mei concedes. Speed, not direction, is the real quarrel.

**—**: ROUND 2 · REBUTTAL

**MODERATOR**: Concrete numbers this round, please. Everyone.

**MODERATOR**: Mei, give us a number. What does this cost?

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Mei's strongest point is sequencing: the pilot evidence is thin on output measurement, so mandate now risks freezing the wrong model. That's fair, and it's why I'd argue for a phased statutory default rather than a single frozen rota. But note what our own compliance data already show: staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error [^7], and the ward that piloted a compressed rota with guaranteed rest days saw burnout fall 19 to 22 percent with throughput, length of stay and readmissions all within normal variation [^8]. Mei's cost question has a number that never gets counted: voluntary nursing resignations at 14 percent, each replacement about four months of salary [^7]. Fund the transition partly from churn we're already paying for. On the money, the honest answer is that the final bill depends on design, and the mechanism to settle it is sector trials with sunset review, not indefinite delay.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: Anybody quoting a single number for this is selling you something. What we can say: in the nine shift-based organisations that actually held coverage constant, the redesign took 18% to 27% more staffed hours, covered by new hires, overtime or agency staff [^9]. Those nine were not hospitals, just clinics, call centres, security, a hotel, a logistics depot, so extrapolate to the ED with care. In continuous-coverage sectors that is a material share of a wage bill, and only two of the nine even tried to measure whether lower sickness and turnover clawed any of it back [^9]. So the honest cost range is wide and design-dependent, which is precisely an argument against mandating it now.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: The strongest point tonight is Amara's, and I'll say so: she's right that sequencing beats a single frozen rota, and she's right that churn is a real cost we're already paying. That deserves an answer, not a wave. But phased because we don't know yet is not phased because we do, and her own remedy — sector trials with sunset review — is my position, not hers. The motion doesn't say run trials, it says adopt nationwide now. So the concession cuts my way. Look at what those trials should be built to fix: survey response fell from 74% to 58% by the final wave, and unhappy workers likely stopped answering, which flatters the results; finance data was self-reported and unaudited; fewer than half used one consistent output measure [^10]. You don't legislate a default on that base. My case is now the boring one: trials where the gap is, in an acute trust, a transport operator and residential care, independently measured, both sides of the ledger counted, published including failures [^11]. Randomise. Then mandate what survives.

**Victor Hale** [happy]: The strongest point from the other side, and I'll name it precisely: the bill in covered hours is real, and any mandate that pretends otherwise is a bad one. Granted. But define the terms of that figure. It is a gross figure, and only two of nine organisations in her own set attempted to net it against sickness, churn and agency spend [^12]. A gross number is the beginning of an accounting question, not the end of a policy question. Now the point she keeps stepping around: the motion says adopt, and adopt means legislate a default standard with a transition, not switch every rota overnight [^13]. Nationwide means the default week in law, not an identical schedule for every employer [^13]. So put my question squarely to the opposition: would you accept a staged timetable, sector trials written into the statute, sunset review, and a clear end point? Because her own remedy, stripped of the word "never", is a timetable — and a timetable is how the two-day weekend arrived: a statutory default with a ten-year runway for agriculture and shipping [^12]. Speed is the quarrel, not destination. Res ipsa loquitur: the thing speaks for itself.

**—**: ROUND 3 · CLOSING

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: I'll answer Mei's point honestly, because she's earned it: she's right that staffing in continuous-coverage sectors costs more, and that our transition month needed six percent more agency hours before it settled back to baseline by week eight [^14]. That's a real number. But notice what the same data show: the pilot wards needed no extra staffed hours long-term, only a two-week planning period and one start date per ward [^14], and rest-day cancellations fell to zero by design, with burnout down roughly a fifth and patient throughput, length of stay and readmissions all within normal variation [^15]. So the recurring cost Mei fears is a transition cost, not a steady-state one, and we're already paying churn we never count. What's still open is ED-scale modelling, which is exactly why I want trials written into the statute with a sunset review. Adopt the default, phase the rollout. That's the motion, and it's the stronger case.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: What's still open is the thing that decides this: whether the recurring cost is real or transitional. We don't know, and neither does the other side. In the nine shift-based organisations the redesign took 18% to 27% more staffed hours just to hold coverage constant, and only two of the nine even tried to measure whether lower sickness and turnover paid any of it back [^16]. Amara now tells us her transition month needed 6% more agency hours and settled by week eight, then calls the recurring cost a transition cost on the strength of that. One month in a ward is not nine sectors at scale, and a two-week planning period is a transition, not the steady state. So yes, she and I agree on the remedy, trials written into the statute with sunset review, randomised where possible, output measured independently, both sides of the ledger counted [^17]. That is my position, and the motion isn't offering us that. It asks the house to adopt the default now, on evidence where fewer than half the firms used one consistent output measure and only two of nine checked the savings. Endorsing the report's own recommendation to run the trials first isn't delay for its own sake, it's refusing to freeze one model before we know which sectors it breaks.

**Victor Hale** [happy]: What remains open is one number, and I will name it: the recurring cost at ED scale. I don't have it and neither do they. But notice what the house is now actually disagreeing about. The opposition's remedy is trials, independently measured, both sides of the ledger, published including failures. So is ours, and we would write that remedy into the statute itself, with a defined point at which the default takes effect. The only live question is whether "we do not yet know" is a reason to legislate a trajectory or a reason to never start one. Every generation's status quo has called itself prudence while billing the future for the cost of standing still. Churn, near-misses, exhaustion — we already pay those, uncounted. The motion does not ask the house to guess the answer. It asks the house to commit to finding it, on a date certain, instead of discovering it by default. Choose the trajectory over the freeze.

**—**: ROUND 4 · VERDICT

**—**: STRONGER CASE: OPPOSITION

## Verdict

Stronger case: opp

The Opposition scored higher on Evidence (9.3 to 8.4), Rebuttal (9.9 to 9.5), and Clarity (9.6 to 8.8), grounding its case in specific pilot gaps and cost figures. The Proposition scored lower on Persuasion (6.3 to 7.5) and could not close the gap between conceding sector trials and defending the motion's demand to adopt nationwide now.
